summaries.example: Imagine a school choosing between two plans for recess. One plan makes a few students very happy but leaves many others unhappy. Another plan gives many students a good, safe time. A utilitarian would compare the results and ask which plan creates the most overall happiness, while counting each student’s happiness as important.
summaries.summary: The history of utilitarianism is the story of an ethical approach that asks people to promote the greatest overall good. It belongs to consequentialism, the family of views that judges actions or policies by their results. Classical utilitarians in the nineteenth century—especially William Godwin, Jeremy Bentham, and John Stuart Mill—developed the approach as a tool for thinking about morality, laws, and social reform. Earlier writers had already discussed happiness, concern for others, and the value of producing good. Bentham gave the theory a clear, secular form: pleasure is good, pain is bad, and choices should be compared by the pleasure and pain they are expected to produce. He also said that the happiness of all affected people should be included. Mill kept the basic focus on happiness but argued that intellectual and more developed pleasures can be better than merely bodily ones. The history also includes disagreements about whether to judge each action directly or to use rules, how much people can be expected to sacrifice, and whether value is only pleasure or includes things such as beauty. The theory has continued to influence moral philosophy, law, and public policy.
key_ideas: Utilitarianism says that the results of an action or rule are central to deciding whether it is right.
Classical utilitarians such as Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill usually treated pleasure and happiness as the good to promote.
Everyone’s happiness counts. Your happiness matters, but it does not automatically matter more than another person’s.
Earlier thinkers, including Mozi, Śāntideva, Hutcheson, Hume, and Godwin, developed ideas that helped lead toward classical utilitarianism.
Bentham tried to compare pleasures and pains by features such as strength, length, likelihood, and the number of people affected.
Mill argued that some pleasures, especially intellectual ones, are better in kind than simple bodily pleasures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Utilitarianism gives people a clear question for judging choices and policies: what effects will this have on everyone involved? It encourages attention to people who might be overlooked and supports examining laws as changeable tools rather than permanent commands. The theory also helps us notice difficult questions about fairness, sacrifice, rules, pleasure, and the treatment of others. Even people who reject utilitarianism can learn from the problems its defenders and critics raise.

important_terms.definition: A way of judging choices by looking mainly at what happens because of them.
The idea that we should choose the option that produces the greatest overall good.
Good experiences, such as enjoyment or happiness, rather than suffering or pain.
Treating everyone’s happiness as equally important, not giving extra weight just because someone is close to you.
A way of measuring how much good or happiness an action produces.

questions_to_think_about: Should a choice that helps many people always beat a choice that helps only one person?
Can following a rule usually create better results than deciding each action separately?
Are all pleasures equally valuable, or might some kinds be better than others?
How should we respond when helping one person greatly would mean helping many others a little?

summaries.example: Suppose a city can spend a fixed amount on either a small project that greatly improves life for a few residents or a larger project that gives a modest benefit to many. A utilitarian comparison would consider the expected intensity, duration, certainty, and extent of the benefits and harms. It would also ask whether a general policy or rule would produce better results over time. The example shows why utilitarian reasoning can require both impartial comparison and difficult judgments about consequences; it does not automatically settle every case.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry traces the development of utilitarianism from earlier theories about happiness and benevolence to the classical nineteenth-century accounts of Godwin, Bentham, and Mill, then to later revisions. Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory: the moral status of an action or policy depends on its consequences. Its distinctive classical commitments are maximization, impartiality, agent-neutrality, and hedonism—the view that pleasure is the basic good and pain the basic bad. Early precursors include theological utilitarians, who grounded duties to promote happiness in God’s will, and moral-sense theorists such as Shaftesbury and Hutcheson, who emphasized sympathy, virtue, and moral judgment. Godwin developed an especially radical, secular, impartial account linked to rational self-direction and social reform. Bentham made utility a practical standard for law and conduct, proposing several dimensions for comparing pleasures and pains. Yet his psychological egoism sits uneasily with a moral requirement to promote general welfare. Mill preserved utility as the ultimate standard but defended qualitative differences among pleasures, appealed to social feelings and internal sanctions, and used utility to support rights, free speech, and women’s political participation. The entry also presents disputes about act and rule standards, total and average utility, demandingness, publicity, and whether intrinsic value includes more than pleasure.
key_ideas: Proto-utilitarian ideas appeared before the nineteenth century, including in ancient Chinese philosophy and medieval Indian philosophy. The classical movement gave related ideas a systematic, secular, and reform-oriented structure.
Godwin defended impartial maximization of good and connected it with rational independence, while also appearing to give an important place to human development rather than simple pleasure.

Bentham combined hedonism with a decision procedure that considers intensity, duration, certainty, proximity, fecundity, purity, and extent. He focused especially on evaluating actions and policies by their effects.

Bentham’s apparent psychological egoism—his claim that people are governed by self-interest—creates tension with a moral standard requiring promotion of everyone’s welfare. His later work appears to allow benevolent motivation.

Mill revised Bentham’s hedonism by distinguishing higher and lower pleasures, emphasizing social feelings and internal sanctions such as conscience, guilt, and remorse. His account of rights and social reform is ultimately justified by utility.

The history raises structural questions: whether Mill is best read as an act- or rule-utilitarian, whether maximizing total or average happiness is correct, and whether value includes non-hedonic goods such as beauty.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history shows that utilitarianism is not one unchanging formula. Its central question—what use will this choice or policy have for overall welfare?—has influenced moral theory, political philosophy, law, and social policy. At the same time, its development exposes serious philosophical pressures: consequences may conflict with rules or rights; maximizing good may demand great sacrifice; psychological motivation may not match moral obligation; and pleasure may not exhaust value. Studying the disagreements among Godwin, Bentham, Mill, Sidgwick, and Moore helps clarify both the power and the limits of outcome-based moral reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A family of ethical theories holding that an action or policy is morally assessed entirely by its consequences or the value it produces.
The classical view that one ought to maximize overall good, with pleasure or happiness treated as the fundamental value.
The view that pleasure is the intrinsic good and pain is the intrinsic bad.
The requirement that each person’s good count equally in the moral calculation.
The idea that the reason one person has to promote overall good is not special to that person; it applies equally to others.
A version of utilitarianism that evaluates an action by the consequences of that action compared with its alternatives.
A version that evaluates actions by the consequences of following the relevant rules or policies.
Value that something has in itself, rather than merely because it produces another valuable result.

questions_to_think_about: If an action produces the best outcome but violates a familiar moral rule, should it be performed?
Does Mill’s distinction between higher and lower pleasures successfully remain a form of hedonism?
Can a theory demand impartial concern for everyone while people are naturally attached to family and friends?
Should a moral theory guide ordinary people directly, or can it recommend simpler rules when calculation is difficult?
If more people have lives worth living but average happiness falls, what should a utilitarian prefer?

summaries.example: A student council has one afternoon to help its school. It can repair a quiet study room for a small group of students or organize a free activity that many students will enjoy. A utilitarian would not simply ask which choice feels nicest to the council members. It would ask which option is likely to create the most happiness overall, including how many students are affected and how long the benefits last. A critic might reply that fairness, promises, or protecting a person’s rights should matter even when breaking them could produce more happiness.
summaries.summary: The history of utilitarianism explains how a moral theory based on overall happiness developed over many centuries. Its basic idea is consequentialist: to judge an action or policy, look at what it produces. Utilitarianism adds a strong requirement of maximization: we should choose the option that creates the greatest total good. It is also impartial, meaning that each person’s welfare counts equally, and agent-neutral, meaning that the reason to help the whole community applies to everyone, not just to a particular person. Earlier thinkers offered pieces of this approach. Some religious writers connected moral duty with God’s wish for human happiness. Others, including Shaftesbury, Hutcheson, and Hume, explored sympathy, moral feeling, and social usefulness. William Godwin developed a radical secular theory that emphasized impartial justice, rational judgment, and reform of government. Jeremy Bentham gave classical utilitarianism its clearest early structure. He identified pleasure as good and pain as bad, and suggested several factors for comparing them. His focus on self-interested human motivation, however, sits awkwardly beside a moral demand to promote general happiness. John Stuart Mill kept the general framework but argued that pleasures differ in quality, not only amount. He also stressed social feelings, conscience, and the role of utility in defending rights and reform. Later debates questioned whether the theory should focus on acts or rules, and whether good means only pleasure.
key_ideas: Utilitarian thought existed before Bentham. Earlier writers discussed happiness, benevolence, sympathy, and concern for the good of a whole community.
The classical approach grew partly from a desire to criticize and reform laws and social practices. It was generally secular and focused on what policies would accomplish.

Bentham treated pleasure and pain as the basic measures of value. He proposed considering strength, duration, likelihood, closeness, future effects, mixture with pain, and the number of people affected.
Bentham’s view creates a puzzle: if people always act from self-interest, how can they be obligated to promote everyone’s happiness when that conflicts with their own?
Mill agreed that happiness is the goal but argued that some pleasures are higher because they involve intellectual and more developed human abilities. He also emphasized conscience and sympathy.
Philosophers have disagreed about whether utilitarianism should judge actions directly, use rules, count total or average happiness, and include values besides pleasure.
summaries.why_it_matters: Utilitarianism matters because it asks moral and political thinkers to take the effects of decisions seriously. It can direct attention toward everyone affected by a law or policy, including people whose interests are easy to ignore. Its history also teaches that a theory may change as philosophers respond to objections. Questions about fairness, rights, promises, sacrifice, pleasure, and social reform remain important whenever people must decide how shared resources and rules should be used.

important_terms.definition: The view that the moral rightness of an action depends on its results.
An ethical theory that says we should maximize the overall good, not merely our own good.
A version of utilitarianism associated especially with Bentham and Mill, centered on happiness or pleasure as the value to promote.
The belief that pleasure is good in itself and pain is bad in itself.
Giving equal moral weight to everyone’s happiness, rather than favoring oneself or one’s friends automatically.
Judging each possible action by its own expected results.
Judging an action by whether the rule behind it would produce good results when generally followed.
Feelings such as guilt or remorse that can motivate people to avoid harming others.

questions_to_think_about: Should a rule against lying be followed if one lie would prevent a serious harm?
Does counting everyone equally require us to ignore special concern for friends and family?
Why might Mill think reading, learning, or solving a hard problem can be better than a simple physical pleasure?
Can a moral theory be fair if it asks people to give up a lot for strangers?
What other things besides happiness might have value?
